claims.claim: Copernicus and the Royal Meteorological Society report that 2024 was 1.60°C above the estimated pre-industrial level.

citations.quote: 2024 is 1.60°C above an estimate of the pre-industrial level, making it the first calendar year to exceed the 1.5°C limit.
citations.note: partly supported: Temperature value supported, but source attribution absent.

citations.quote: This is equivalent to 1.60°C above an estimate of the 1850-1900 temperature designated to be the pre-industrial level.
citations.note: partly supported: Royal Meteorological Society absent; Copernicus and 1.60°C confirmed.

claims.quote: 2024 is 1.60°C above an estimate of the pre-industrial level, making it the first calendar year to exceed the 1.5°C limit.

claims.claim: The World Meteorological Organization’s consolidated analysis of six datasets gives 1.55°C, with a margin of uncertainty of ±0.13°C, above the 1850–1900 average.

citations.quote: The global average surface temperature was 1.55 °C (with a margin of uncertainty of ± 0.13 °C) above the 1850-1900 average, according to WMO’s consolidated analysis of the six datasets.
citations.note: another passage on the page may disagree: "To calculate the consolidated figures for temperatures relative to pre-industrial, WMO calculates anomalies relative to 1981-2010 for each dataset and then adds"

claims.quote: The global average surface temperature was 1.55 °C (with a margin of uncertainty of ± 0.13 °C) above the 1850-1900 average, according to WMO’s consolidated analysis of the six datasets.

claims.claim: NASA estimates 2024 was about 1.47°C warmer than the mid-19th century average, while NOAA puts the figure at 1.46°C above the pre-industrial average.

citations.quote: NASA scientists further estimate Earth in 2024 was about 2.65 degrees Fahrenheit (1.47 degrees Celsius) warmer than the mid-19th century average (1850-1900).
citations.note: partly supported: No passage mentions NOAA's 1.46°C estimate; only NASA supported.

citations.quote: The global average surface temperature was 2.32 Fahrenheit (1.29 degrees Celsius) above the 20th-century average (57.0 degrees Fahrenheit, or 13.9 degrees Celsius) and 2.63 degrees Fahrenheit (1.46 degrees Celsius) above the pre-industrial average (56.7 degrees Fahrenheit, or 13.7 degrees Celsius), which NOAA defines as the period from 1850-1900.
citations.note: partly supported: Only NOAA figure supported; NASA estimate absent from passages.
